title: streaming-sse-chunking-backpressure-debug-notes-maya-singh
content:
Notes and repro for intermittent streaming issues (SSE / chunked transfer / backpressure)

Context:
- Seeing sporadic client stalls when streaming long responses from the Redwood streaming endpoint (hosted API / internal test infra). Symptoms include: client receives initial chunks then connection hangs for long time (>10s) before remaining chunks arrive, or connection resets with "connection reset by peer".
- Affected clients: browser EventSource, Node fetch with streaming, Python requests/httpx.
- Suspected interaction between runtime, reverse proxy (nginx/internal LB), and client backpressure semantics.

Repro objective:
- Provide small, repeatable repro that demonstrates: (1) chunks being buffered/delayed by intermediary, (2) backpressure when client cannot read quickly, (3) potential large initial chunk causing pause.

Environments tried:
- Local dev server (Express) -> direct client: works as expected (immediate chunks).
- Local dev server behind nginx (default proxy_buffering on): reproduces delay/buffering.
- Internal staging service (our runtime) behind internal LB + envoy: reproduce intermittently.

Commands and quick repros:
1) curl SSE simple test against local express server (works):

$ curl -N http://localhost:3000/stream
# -N disables buffering on curl side so it flushes as it receives

2) curl against nginx-proxied endpoint (shows buffering):

$ curl -N http://localhost:8080/stream
# Observed: first chunk arrives, then nothing for ~5-10s, then a burst of chunks.

3) curl with verbose to inspect headers:

$ curl -v -N http://localhost:8080/stream
> GET /stream HTTP/1.1
> Host: localhost:8080
> Accept: */*
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< content-type: text/event-stream
< transfer-encoding: chunked
< cache-control: no-cache

Hypothesis: nginx proxy_buffering is enabled and collects up to proxy_buffers before sending; small flushes from backend may be coalesced. Also gzip or other filters can cause buffering.

Server-side minimal Node repro (server flushes small chunks):

const http = require('http')
http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/event-stream', 'Cache-Control': 'no-cache' })
  let i = 0
  const t = setInterval(() => {
    i++
    res.write(`data: chunk ${i}\n\n`)
    if (i === 20) { clearInterval(t); res.end() }
  }, 200)
}).listen(3000)

- Direct to browser EventSource this is smooth. Behind nginx, first 3 chunks then long pause.

Things tried / results:
- nginx: set proxy_buffering off; result: fixes buffering in test environment.
- nginx: add proxy_set_header X-Accel-Buffering no; result: sometimes helpful with upstreams like gunicorn.
- disabled gzip on nginx and on upstream; result: reduced buffering.
- adjusted proxy_buffer_size and proxy_buffers; increases reduced pauses but didn't eliminate in staging.
- toggled keepalive_timeout and chunked_transfer_encoding settings on upstream; mixed results.

Observed error snippets:
- Client console (browser): "EventSource connection lost" then reconnect, sometimes with partial streams.
- Node client: Error: socket hang up (stack trace shows ECONNRESET) when upstream closes mid-stream after long inactivity.
- nginx logs: upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream

Hypotheses and notes:
1) Backpressure semantics: if client stops reading (e.g., slow consumer), TCP window shrinks, upstream write() blocks or OS buffers fill. Our runtime may not be configured to block or to handle backpressure gracefully; it could be queuing writes in memory and then hitting resource limits, leading to reset.
2) Proxy buffering + filters: nginx/envoy can buffer small writes until thresholds. This makes streaming appear bursty. Turning off buffering or tuning buffer sizes helps.
3) Large initial chunk: one test where backend sent a ~64KB initial JSON (metadata) then started streaming tokens — proxies sometimes hold the large chunk and don't flush the tiny follow-ups until the initial buffer is drained. Solution: send small initial handshake and flush, or use explicit SSE event boundaries and call flush.
4) TLS termination / ALB interaction: some LBs will buffer and re-chunk; need to verify ALB/NLB config.

Experiments to run in staging (actionable):
- Add a small initial event ("event: ready\ndata: ready\n\n") and force flush; observe if client sees immediate readiness before token stream.
- On runtime side, ensure responses call flush() after every event (in languages that support it).
- Deploy build with instrumentation: log timestamps for write() returns and for flush completion at runtime and log write durations. Compare with time of client receipt (via client-side timestamps).
- Reproduce with tcpdump at proxy to confirm whether delayed bursts are between backend->proxy or proxy->client. Capture pcap for the two directions.

Repro steps (minimal):
1) Start test server (Node example above) on :3000.
2) Start nginx reverse proxy with default config on :8080 proxy_pass to :3000.
3) curl -N http://localhost:8080/stream (observe delay).
4) Edit nginx conf: add "proxy_buffering off;" in location block, reload, and re-run curl. Expect immediate streaming.

Additional commands used to inspect buffering and TCP state:
- ss -tanp | grep 8080  # look for sockets in CLOSE_WAIT / TIME_WAIT
- sudo tcpdump -i any port 8080 -w /tmp/streaming.pcap  # capture and open in wireshark
- strace -p <pid_of_runtime> -e write  # see write syscalls blocking

Notes on client-side consumption shaping backpressure:
- Browsers: EventSource automatically processes events; but if onmessage handler is heavy (sync CPU work), that will stall UI thread and delay reading. Recommend offloading heavy work to WebWorker or queueing minimal processing until stream completes.
- Node: if consumer is piping to a slow writable stream, writable.write() returns false when downstream is saturated; caller should pause writes until 'drain'. Ensure our runtime obeys this and does not ignore backpressure signals.

Potential fixes / mitigations:
- In runtime: honor backpressure: check stream.write() return and wait for 'drain' event; avoid unlimited buffering. Add per-connection memory caps.
- Force small initial flush + no large initial payloads.
- Configure proxies: proxy_buffering off for streaming routes, disable gzip, tune buffer sizes. For envoy, set 'use_remote_address' and 'streaming' options appropriately.
- Add explicit SSE keepalive comments (":\n") every few seconds to keep proxies from closing idle streams.

Next steps (TODO):
- Reproduce reliably in staging with capture and timeline. (Assigned to Samir)
- Add write/flush instrumentation to runtime and deploy to canary. (Assigned to Evan)
- Draft RFC for streaming SLOs + proxy configuration recommendations for customers.

Scratchpad of commands used during session (copyable):
- start server: node server.js
- proxy: sudo nginx -c /etc/nginx/nginx-stream-test.conf -s reload
- curl: curl -v -N http://localhost:8080/stream
- tcpdump: sudo tcpdump -i any port 8080 -w /tmp/streaming.pcap
- strace: sudo strace -p <pid> -e write

If anyone else hits this please add notes here (what LB/proxy, gzipping, client type). I think the most actionable immediate mitigation is turning off proxy buffering for streaming endpoints and ensuring runtime honors backpressure.
